(1) According to the reviewer's suggestion, we have added the in situ NAP-XPS results of Ti and O orbitals in the revised manuscript. Although the shifts in Ti and O are less pronounced than those of Ni and Ir (given that the actual loading of Ni-Ir is below 2 wt.% relative to the TiO support), they still provide supporting evidence for the electron transfer pathway. In situ NAP-XPS of Ti 2p and O 1s (Supplementary Fig. 24d-e) reveal the positive shift in the binding energy of Ti and O under light irradiation, indicating electron migration from the TiO support to the Ni-Ir sites under illumination. Moreover, in the activity test section, we compared TiO with a non-photocatalytic semiconductor support, SiO . Comparative tests on NiIr /TiO and NiIr /SiO (Supplementary Fig. 14 and Note 2) further confirmed that TiO -supported NiIr nanoclusters uniquely harness coupled photothermal-photoelectric effects to achieve efficient and stable DRM catalysis. This comparison underscores the essential role of the TiO support under illumination.
(2) In addition, while we appreciate the reviewer's attention to this point, we would like to note that the evidence for the direction of electron transfer is not exclusively based on the in situ NAP-XPS spectra. In situ XAS analysis (Fig. 3a-c and Supplementary Figs. 18-20 in the revised version) also corroborates this electron migration pathway. In the mechanism discussion, we also analyzed the time-decay fitting of the transient absorption signal at 560 nm (Fig. 4h and Supplementary Fig. 39d-f in the revised version), which revealed a 520.3 fs lifetime for NiIr /TiO , markedly longer than TiO (110.9 fs) or Ni/TiO (233.1 fs), directly evidencing retarded charge recombination via Ni-Ir interaction. DFT calculations (Fig. 4i in the revised version) further show that electrons in photoexcited states preferentially accumulate at Ir sites distal to the TiO interface. S →S promotes hole accumulation at Ni sites alongside electron enrichment at Ir sites, a spatial charge segregation that drives photoexcited electrons toward Ir centers in higher-energy states. Related explanations were also provided in our response to your Comment 2.
(3) We also sincerely thank the reviewer for the valuable comments regarding the seemingly overlapping peaks in the Ir 4f XPS spectra. We fully understand the concern and would like to clarify that the partially overlapping features of Ir are intrinsic to the nature of its 4f core levels and to the coexistence of multiple oxidation states in our catalyst, rather than a result of inappropriate fitting.
First, the Ir 4f region is inherently complex. The Ir 4f core level consists of two spin-orbit components, Ir 4f and Ir 4f , with a relatively consistent spin-orbit splitting. In our NiIr /TiO system, three oxidation states of Ir coexist. The metallic Ir0 component is located at around 60.4-60.6 eV (4f ) and 62.9-63.2 eV (4f ), while Ir4+ appears at 61.5-61.7 and 63.9-64.2, and Ir3+ at approximately 62.2-62.4 eV and 65.1-65.3 eV. The chemical shifts among these species are relatively small, typically less than 1 eV, which is comparable to or even smaller than the experimental energy resolution of Al Kα radiation. As a result, the six sub-peaks corresponding to these three oxidation states (each consisting of two spin-orbit doublets) exhibit a certain degree of overlap, but no individual peak completely envelopes another individual peak. This spectral convolution is well recognized in many reports on Ir-based oxides and supported Ir catalysts (e.g., Science 387,791-796(2025); Nat. Commun. 16, 181 (2025); Cited from J. Am. Chem. Soc. 146. 19327-19336 (2024)), all showing similarly Ir 4f peaks.
It is also important to note that Ir3+ sometimes exhibits slightly higher binding energy than Ir4+, which may appear counterintuitive. This behavior has been widely discussed and is attributed to final-state screening effects and the covalent character of Ir-O bonds. In Ir3+ environments, stronger Ir-O hybridization weakens the screening of the core hole, leading to a higher apparent binding energy compared with the more ionic Ir4+ species. Therefore, the small energetic overlap between Ir3+ and Ir4+ components and their reversed binding energy order are both physically reasonable and consistent with the literature (Science 387,791-796(2025); Nat. Commun. 16, 181 (2025); Cited from J. Am. Chem. Soc. 146. 19327-19336 (2024)).
Regarding the fitting procedure, our peak deconvolution was performed using the Xpeak software, and it strictly followed standard and reproducible XPS fitting principles. The spin-orbit splitting for each Ir component was fixed, and the area ratio of Ir 4f to Ir 4f was constrained to 4:3 according to their theoretical degeneracy. The full width at half maximum (FWHM) was kept consistent across different oxidation states within the same sample, and a Shirley background was applied. The peak profiles were modeled using a Gaussian-Lorentzian (GL(30)) line shape, which is widely used for transition-metal XPS analysis. To further demonstrate the robustness of the fitting, we have provided representative fitting-parameter screenshots and numerical fitting tables from XPEAK in below figure, confirming that all components were treated under uniform and physically meaningful constraints.
Furthermore, even without detailed deconvolution, the evolution of the raw Ir 4f spectra itself clearly supports our interpretation. As indicated by the green arrows in Fig. 3d below, the intensity near 60.6 eV, corresponding to the Ir 4f component of metallic Ir0, gradually increases from the dark condition to the unfocused light and then to the focused light conditions. This visible enhancement in the low-binding-energy shoulder directly evidences the photo-induced reduction of Ir species and the generation of additional metallic Ir0 domains under illumination, which is in excellent agreement with the quantitative increase of the Ir0 fraction obtained from the fitted peak areas.

In summary, the apparent overlap of Ir 4f peaks is an intrinsic characteristic of Ir due to the small energy separation among its oxidation states and spin–orbit components. Our XPS fitting performed with XPEAK strictly followed accepted conventions and yielded physically meaningful and self-consistent results. The trend observed in the raw spectra independently confirms the light-induced enrichment of metallic Ir0, further validating the correctness and reliability of our XPS interpretation.

Comment 7: Why does the photoelectric effect disappear when the light intensity larger than 3.89 W/cm2, and how to distinguish the contribution of photoelectric effect and photothermal effect? And how is the TAVG (average surface temperature of the catalyst) in Figure 1d calculated?
Reply: We sincerely thank the reviewer for this valuable comment, which has helped us further clarify and improve the manuscript.
(1) We would like to clarify that the photoelectric effect does not disappear when the light intensity exceeds 3.89 W cm-2. As the light intensity increases further, the catalyst's photon absorption reaches saturation. Consequently, the excess light energy is increasingly converted into thermal energy, making the thermal effect more pronounced. This explains why in Fig. 2d (the original Fig. 1d), we observe that while the actual surface temperature of the catalyst continues to rise as the light intensity increases from 3.89 W cm-2 to 4.27 W cm-2 and beyond, the activity contribution per unit light intensity (left Y-axis) begins to decrease. We consider 3.89 W cm-2 to be the light intensity that offers the optimal utilization of the photoelectric effect. At higher intensities, while the photoelectric effect still exists, we emphasize that the thermal contribution becomes increasingly dominant in the overall reaction. Regarding this point, we have provided the explanation in the manuscript, "Beyond 4.27 W cm-2, photon absorption saturation redirected excess energy into thermal pathways, diminishing the per-unit-light efficiency despite continued temperature increases (T > 600 °C). This nonlinear response highlights the delicate balance between photocarriers generation and thermal dissipation in light-driven systems." Regarding Fig. 2d (the original Fig. 1d), we have also addressed this in our response of your Comment 8.
(2) Distinguishing the contributions of the photoelectric effect and the photothermal effect has always been a challenge in light-driven catalytic reactions, especially in systems like ours without external heating, where light induces both effects. Nevertheless, this study includes corresponding experimental designs to differentiate them appropriately.
Firstly, in Fig. 2d (the original Fig. 1d), by calculating the activity contribution per unit light intensity, we indicated that the light intensity range where the photoelectric effect plays a significant role is < 1.95 W cm-2. As the light intensity increases further, the photoelectric and photothermal effects act synergistically, leading to the rapid rise in activity observed (1.95-3.89 W cm-2). When the light intensity exceeds 3.89 W cm-2, photon absorption becomes saturated. Although the photothermal effect continues to increase, the rate of increase in CH and CO conversion rates beyond 3.89 W cm-2 becomes more gradual compared to the range of 1.95-3.89 W cm-2. This indirectly suggests that the increase in the photothermal effect contributes less to the activity boost than the increase in the photoelectric effect does within that optimal range.
To further distinguish which effect contributes more during the rapid activity increase phase, we conducted the condensation equipment experiment shown in Fig. 2e (the original Fig. 1e). The blue trend line in Fig. 2e represents the results under a constant light intensity of 3.89 W cm-2, while condensate (the temperature of the condensate is marked in blue font) were circulated around the reactor to achieve cooling. The X-axis records the real-time monitored temperature at the catalyst's center point. This setup allows us to observe the DRM activity and H /CO ratio while maintaining the photoelectric effect (constant light intensity) and reducing the photothermal effect (via condensation). For comparison, the yellow trend line in Fig. 2e represents the results obtained by directly varying the light intensity without extra condensation. This simultaneously reduces both the photoelectric and photothermal effects (different light intensity values are marked in yellow font), with the X-axis showing the actual temperature monitored at the catalyst's center resulting from the reduced light intensity. By comparing the yellow and blue trend lines at matched catalyst surface center temperatures, we can estimate the contributions that the variation along the blue trend line allows calculation of the activity contribution from the photoelectric effect, while the yellow trend line reflects the combined contribution of photoelectric and photothermal effects. As stated in the manuscript, "At matched surface temperatures, the photoelectric-dominated system contributed 57.5% to syngas rates and 91.7% to H /CO balance, compared to the photothermal-assisted system." That is to say, the photothermal effect contributed only about 42.5% to the syngas production rate and 8.3% to the H /CO balance under these conditions. These results demonstrate the dominant role of the photoelectric effect in this system.
Additionally, in the Supplementary Information, we compared a non-photocatalytic semiconductor, SiO as the support. " Comparative tests on NiIr /TiO and NiIr /SiO (Supplementary Fig. 14 and Note 2) further confirmed that TiO -supported NiIr nanoclusters uniquely harness coupled photothermal-photoelectric effects to achieve efficient and stable DRM catalysis." This result again emphasizes the significance of the photoelectric effect.
The reviewer's question may arise because our original description of Fig. 2e was perhaps not sufficiently detailed. Therefore, we have revised the manuscript to provide a more detailed explanation of the related content.
(3) Regarding the calculation of T (average surface temperature of the catalyst) in Fig. 1d (now Fig. 2d): The built-in thermocouple position is movable. The average surface temperature was calculated by measuring temperatures at five different points on the catalyst surface (as shown below).
In Fig. 2d, we labeled both T (the average temperature of catalyst surface)and T (the center temperature of catalyst surface)to comprehensively represent the catalyst surface temperature distribution. Since the temperature at the catalyst center is the highest, T is used for investigation and analysis elsewhere in the paper.
We have also supplemented infrared IR thermal imaging data (Supplementary Fig. 13) which verified the accuracy of our temperature measurement method. We hope this clarification satisfactorily addresses the reviewer's concern. Furthermore, we have provided a more detailed description of the temperature measurement methodology in the Methods section.

Comment 8: There are some conclusions without evidence or reference in the manuscript, such as “Activity surged above a threshold light intensity of 2 W cm-2, marking the onset of photoelectric-photothermal synergy (Fig. 1d)”, and “Beyond 4.27 W cm-2, photon absorption saturation redirected excess energy into thermal pathways, diminishing the per-unit-light efficiency despite continued temperature increases (T > 600 °C).” There is no reference or experimental evidence to support these conclusions.
Reply: We thank the reviewer for pointing this out, enabling us to improve our manuscript.
(1) The conclusion that "Activity surged above a threshold light intensity of 2 W cm-2, marking the onset of photoelectric-photothermal synergy" is in fact supported by experimental evidence. As shown in Fig. 2d (originally Fig. 1d), when the light intensity is below 2 W cm-2, the catalyst surface center temperature (T ) and average temperature (T ) remain below 350 °C. Referring to Fig. 2c and Supplementary Fig. 12a, thermal catalytic experiments under dark conditions show almost no H or CO production when the temperature is below 350 °C, indicating negligible thermal catalytic activity in this range. Therefore, under illumination without external heating, when the photothermal heating remains below 350 °C, the contribution can be primarily attributed to the photoelectric effect. As the light intensity increases beyond 2 W cm-2, the thermal effect from illumination becomes non‐negligible, which is why we describe the regime beyond this point as photoelectric-photothermal synergy.
(2) The statement "Beyond 4.27 W cm-2, photon absorption saturation redirected excess energy into thermal pathways, diminishing the per-unit-light efficiency despite continued temperature increases (T > 600 °C)" is also experimentally substantiated. From Fig. 2d (the original Fig. 1d), we observe that although the actual surface temperature of the catalyst continues to rise as light intensity increases beyond 3.89 W cm-2 to 4.27 W cm-2 and further, the activity per unit light intensity (left Y-axis) begins to decline. This occurs because the catalyst has a finite capacity for photon absorption. Once the light intensity exceeds a certain level, the catalyst reaches photon absorption saturation. At this stage, the photoelectric contribution no longer increases significantly with light intensity, whereas the photothermal effect continues to increase. Therefore, beyond 4.27 W cm-2, the increase in overall activity is mainly attributed to the thermal effect, and the per-unit-light efficiency (syngas generation rates/light intensity) decreases. This clearly indicates that photon absorption saturation redirects excess energy into thermal pathways, thereby reducing per-unit-light efficiency despite the continued rise in temperature. Therefore, 3.89 W cm-2 can be regarded as the light intensity that achieves optimal utilization of the photoelectric effect. At higher intensities, we do not deny the presence of the photoelectric effect, but emphasize that the thermal effect becomes increasingly dominant in the reaction.
We recognize that the original expression was perhaps too concise, potentially causing confusion for the reviewer. To address this, we have provided more detailed elaboration on these aspects in the revised manuscript.

Comment 10: The explanation for Figure 1 f is too simplistic. Under the full-spectrum condition, both the Ir and Ni surfaces can be excited by light to generate hot electrons. Moreover, Fig 1f shows Ir has a stronger light absorption ability to than Ni. Will the LSPR effect on Ir trigger the transfer of hot electrons to Ni?
Reply: We sincerely thank the reviewer for this valuable comment, which has helped us further clarify and improve the manuscript. Regarding the light absorption ability, Supplementary Fig. 15a shows that the monometallic Ir/TiO exhibits slightly stronger absorption than Ni/TiO , though the difference is not substantial. This moderate enhancement may be attributed to the intrinsic properties of noble metals. Furthermore, light absorption is also influenced by metal loading. In the NiIr/TiO series, while the Ni loading remains essentially constant, the total metal loading increases with higher Ir/Ni ratios (as shown in Supplementary Fig. 1). Consequently, the overall light absorption capacity of the NiIr/TiO catalysts is further enhanced.
Regarding Fig. 2f (the original Fig. 1f), it demonstrates that the wavelength-dependent DRM activity (per W·cm-2) of NiIr /TiO aligns with its UV-Vis-NIR absorption profile. This strong correlation confirms that the reaction is primarily driven by photoexcitation rather than thermal effects, as the activity directly follows the photons absorbed by the catalyst. We have enhanced the corresponding description in the revised manuscript.
As for the electron transfer pathway, our mechanistic investigations have demonstrated that under illumination, electrons are transferred from Ni to Ir sites. In situ NAP-XPS analyses provide direct evidence of this light-induced electron transfer. The Ir 4f spectra (Fig. 3d-e) reveal a pronounced shift toward lower binding energy, with the Ir0 fraction increasing from 36.96% (dark) to 60.65%. Upon switching to focused light, the Ir0 fraction further rises to 62.31%. This indicates that Ir gains electrons under irradiation. Parallel in situ Ni 2p NAP-XPS (Supplementary Fig. 24a-c) shows analogous trends, with Ni0/Ni2+ ratios tracking Ir's redox dynamics. While Ti 2p and O 1s exhibit the positive shift in the binding energy of Ti and O under light irradiation (Supplementary Fig. 24d-e), this demonstrates that electrons migrate from the TiO support to Ni-Ir under illumination. Subsequently, electrons are further transferred from Ni to Ir. In situ XAS analysis (Fig. 3a-c, Supplementary Fig. 19-20, and Supplementary Tables 4-5) also supports this mechanism. It reveals that Ir in the alloy phase does not directly interact with TiO , while Ni maintains interfacial Ni-O bonds, forming a nano-island structure that isolates the NiIr alloy from the support. This configuration formation indicates the electron transfer from Ni to Ir under light irradiation. Additionally, time-dependent DFT (TD-DFT) simulations (Fig. 4i) show that electrons in photoexcited states preferentially accumulate at Ir sites distal to the TiO interface. S →S promotes hole accumulation at Ni sites alongside electron enrichment at Ir sites, a spatial charge segregation that drives photoexcited electrons toward Ir centers in higher-energy states.

Response to Reviewer 2
General comments: This paper investigates the structural dynamic evolution of NiIr/TiO under light irradiation, which represents a critical challenge in light-driven catalysis. Furthermore, the NiIr/TiO system demonstrates comprehensively favorable efficiency in the dry reforming of methane reaction, with its anti-coking mechanism thoroughly explained. The authors' elegant experimental design using condensation equipment and light intensity thresholds to deconvolute photoelectric and thermal effects is methodologically sound and mechanistically informative. Overall, this work is innovative, and the experimental results sufficiently support the conclusions. Therefore, I recommend this paper for acceptance in Nature Communications after the following revisions.
Reply: We appreciate the reviewer for the careful reading and the generous recommendation of our manuscript. The suggestions and comments have been carefully considered, and we made the corresponding revision to address the points the reviewer has raised, as shown below. We hope our revision can make the paper much more acceptable for publication in the Nature Communications.
Comment 1: In the catalyst preparation section, the authors state: "By conducting the adsorption process in an aprotic solvent and introducing an anionic Ir precursor complexed with quaternary ammonium, we minimized competitive adsorption of Ni and Ir and effectively reduced metal leaching." Please clarify the specific role of the quaternary ammonium in this process. Explain why IrCl could not be used directly for targeted adsorption instead of the complexed precursor. If this strategy effectively overcomes the drawbacks of conventional co-impregnation methods, its clear explanation will provide valuable guidance for future synthesis.
Reply: We thank the reviewer for this insightful comment. Regarding the adsorption of Ir and Ni precursors on the TiO surface, our approach was inspired by a previously reported strategy (Science 362, 560-564 (2018)), which employs sequential adsorption of cationic and anionic species. As described in the Methods section, the surface of the alkalized TiO was first treated with an aqueous NiCl solution. To promote interaction between the Ir precursor and the pre-adsorbed Ni sites, we subsequently used an anionic Ir complex, Na IrCl . This enables electrostatic anchoring of the Ir species around the Ni sites via cation-anionic interaction. In contrast, IrCl exists predominantly in cationic form in aqueous solution and would not be suitable for this targeted adsorption strategy.
The role of the quaternary ammonium cations (tetrabutylammonium, TBA⁺) is to facilitate phase transfer of the IrCl 3- anions from the aqueous phase into an aprotic organic solvent (CH Cl ). This process enhances the stability of the Ir precursor and allows for controlled, slow adsorption, thereby minimizing unwanted ripening or leaching of Ir that could occur in an aqueous environment.
We have provided a detailed description of this preparation procedure in the Methods section. In addition, as suggested, we have now included a clearer explanation of the role of the quaternary ammonium cations in the revised manuscript to better highlight the advantages of this synthetic strategy.

Synthesis and atomic-scale structural analysis of partially oxidized NiIr nanoclusters on TiO .
To construct bimetallic NiIr nanoclusters on TiO with precise atomic pairing, we adopted a directional adsorption strategy23 (Fig. 1a; see Methods for synthesis details). This approach leverages sequential electrostatic adsorption of cationic Ni complexes and anionic Ir precursors onto alkalized TiO nanosheets, ensuring preferential Ir anchoring onto pre-adsorbed Ni sites. For the Ir precursor, we used a species complexed with quaternary ammonium cations to enable its phase transfer into an aprotic solvent. This controlled process prevents Ir ripening and leaching. Consequently, by conducting adsorption in this manner, we minimized competitive adsorption of Ni and Ir, effectively overcoming a key limitation of conventional co-impregnation methods.
Subsequent H calcination eliminated organic ligands while strengthening Ni-Ir metallic interactions, yielding ultrafine bimetallic clusters with uniform dispersion on the TiO support (Fig. 1b). Inductively coupled plasma-atomic emission spectrometry (ICP-AES) confirms controlled metal loadings across NiIrₓ/TiO samples (Supplementary Fig. 1 and Table S1), where x denotes the Ir/Ni theoretical atomic ratio. The sublinear increase in Ir/Ni ratios with x suggests saturation of Ir adsorption onto pre-adsorbed Ni sites, excluding independent Ir deposition. For comparison, monometallic Ni/TiO and Ir/TiO were prepared with a theoretical loading of 1 wt.% for each metal.
Aberration-corrected high-angle annular dark-field scanning transmission electron microscopy (HAADF-STEM) analysis revealed that Ni species or Ir species on TiO exhibited sub-1.2 nm clusters (Supplementary Figs. 2-3), whereas the NiIr nanoclusters on TiO showed an increase in size, progressively reaching up to 1.61 nm with higher Ir content (Supplementary Figs. 4). This trend supports the co-stabilization of Ni and Ir atoms within the bimetallic clusters. This size evolution directly supports the formation of bimetallic NiIr nanoclusters, as the incorporation of Ir stabilizes the clusters and promotes their growth. Atomic-scale characterization of NiIr /TiO provided further insights into the spatial distribution of Ni and Ir atoms. Filtered and color-coded HAADF-STEM images and the corresponding intensity profiles (Fig. 1c-d, Supplementary Fig. 5b-c) revealed intertwined Ni-Ir distributions within individual clusters. The 3D surface plot of a selected region (Fig. 1f) highlighted Ir atoms (whitish-yellow peaks within blue dashed marks) surrounding Ni atoms (darker yellow bumps), demonstrating cohesive bimetallic nanocluster formation. Conversely, monometallic samples exhibited only metal-TiO contrast (Supplementary Figs. 2g-h, 3e-f). Moreover, EDS line scans (Fig.1g) and elemental mapping (Fig. 1h and Supplementary Fig. 5d-i) confirmed the intimate contact between Ni and Ir atoms. Owing to the higher atomic ratio of Ni to Ir, trace amounts of isolated Ni species inevitably persist. Crucially, all Ir atoms preferentially occupy Ni-associated sites, with no detectable isolated Ir single atoms observed on the TiO support (Fig. 1b).
Next, we elucidate the chemical structure and coordination environment of the NiIr nanoclusters.
X-ray Diffraction (XRD) patterns confirm exclusive anatase-phase TiO (Supplementary Fig. 6), with no detectable reflections from metallic Ni or Ir phases, consistent with HAADF-STEM evidence of dispersed sub-2 nm clusters. Normalized Ir L₃-edge and Ni K-edge X-ray absorption near-edge spectroscopy (XANES) analysis reveal partially oxidized states of Ni and Ir (Supplementary Fig.7a-b). Linear combination fitting (Supplementary Fig. 7c-d) shows higher Ir oxidation in Ir/TiO (+3.6) than NiIr /TiO (+2.7), and more reduced Ni in Ni/TiO (+1.6) versus NiIr /TiO (+1.8), indicating electron transfer from Ni to Ir, later corroborated by in situ analyses.
Extended X-ray absorption fine structure (EXAFS) at the Ir L₃-edge provides atomic-scale coordination details (Fig. 1i). All samples exhibit a prominent peak at ~1.60 Å and a relatively weaker peak at ~2.56 Å, corresponding to Ir-O scattering and Ir-Ir scattering, respectively. Notably, NiIr /TiO samples exhibit an additional peak at 2.18 Å, which can be attributed to Ni-Ir scattering.
These results demonstrate that NiIr nanoclusters exhibit a partially oxidized state, with electronic modulation between Ni and Ir atoms. The partial oxidation probably arises from the interface reconstruction between nanocluster and the surface lattice O atoms of TiO during the calcination process and the exposure to air during storage. This unique electronic structure, coupled with their ultrafine size, positions these partially oxidized NiIr nanoclusters (Ox-NiIr) as promising candidates for the adsorption of CH and CO due to their inherent thermal instability19.
In situ CO probe molecule diffuse reflectance infrared Fourier transform spectroscopy (DRIFTS) analyses were conducted to unravel the surface structure and adsorption behavior of NiIr nanoclusters (Supplementary Fig. 8 and Fig. 1j). Ni/TiO₂ exhibited negligible *CO chemisorption signals (<2100 cm⁻¹), which vanished entirely upon heating to 100 ℃. This confirms the inadequacy of individual Ni sites for CO adsorption. In contrast, Ir-containing samples (NiIrₓ/TiO , Ir/TiO ) display intense *CO chemisorption bands (2100-1990 cm⁻¹), with adsorption strength scaling with Ir content. Heating-up desorption revealed a volcanic trend: *CO intensity peaked at 200 ℃ and declined continuously to 400 ℃. It demonstrates reversible CO binding, which is a critical feature for sustaining DRM activity. Detailed comparison of the desorption spectra at 25 ℃ (Fig. 1j) highlights distinct Ir coordination environments. For Ir/TiO₂, three CO species were resolved: (i) multi-carbonyl Ir-(CO) (2068 cm-¹, low-coordination sites)24, (ii) linear CO on metallic Ir (Ir-CO, 2033 cm-¹)25, and (iii) bridged CO at Ir-TiO interfaces (Ir -CO, 1994 cm-¹)26. For Ni/TiO₂, only weak peaks of Ni-CO and Ni -CO can be observed. In NiIr /TiO , the dominant Ir-(CO) peak progressively shifts downward (2063→2044 cm-¹) with increasing Ir content, signaling enhanced π-backdonation from Ir to CO. The observed redshift arises from Ni-to-Ir electron transfer, which elevates Ir's d-orbital occupancy, strengthens Ir-C bonds, and weakens C-O bonds. These results confirm that in partially oxidized NiIr nanoclusters, Ir serves as the main center for CO adsorption, while Ni modulates Ir's electronic properties to optimize the balance between adsorption strength and desorption kinetics.

Comment 3: The accuracy of temperature measurement is critical for understanding photothermal effects. The authors used a thermocouple to monitor the catalyst temperature, but significant thermal resistance between the gas phase and the thermocouple may lead to inaccurate readings, as noted. It is necessary to clarify the detailed setup of temperature measurement (e.g., thermocouple position, calibration methods) or explain how potential thermal resistance effects were mitigated. Additionally, whether complementary methods such as infrared thermography were used to verify the measured temperatures should be addressed.
Reply: We thank the reviewer for the insightful comment. In response to the concern about potential thermal resistance between the gas phase and the thermocouple, we would like to clarify our experimental setup and validation approach.
In contrast to many reported studies where the thermocouple is placed at the bottom of the catalyst bed or even further away, which may not fully capture the direct photothermal heating effect on the upper catalyst surface. In our configuration, the thermocouple probe was placed in direct contact with the upper surface of the catalyst at its center (T ), allowing us to capture the highest local temperature under irradiation (as shown by the red indicator line representing the thermocouple in Supplementary Fig. 9). This arrangement minimizes the thermal resistance effect by avoiding indirect measurement through the gas phase or reactor materials. It is also worth noting that, since gas molecules typically adsorb and react on the catalyst surface, measuring the temperature at the upper surface is a reasonable approach for evaluating the actual reaction conditions. A type-K thermocouple (0-1150 °C range, 0.5 mm diameter, ±0.1 °C accuracy) was embedded in the quartz sand bed, with a 90°-bent tip protruding 1.0 mm above the surface. This high-precision thermocouple was selected to reduce measurement deviation. Regarding calibration, the thermocouple was pre-calibrated against standard reference sources, and its performance was verified at multiple temperature setpoints to ensure consistency across the experimental range. In Methods section, we provided a more detailed description of this device in the revised version. To further address any concerns about thermal resistance and measurement reliability, we performed complementary temperature validation using infrared (IR) thermography. The results obtained from the IR camera showed agreement with the thermocouple results, confirming that our temperature measurement approach is both accurate and reliable.

Reply: We thank the reviewer for their careful observation. Your comment regarding the Y-axis value exceeding 1 in Fig. 2f (the original Fig. 1f) is pertinent, as this is indeed a common point of discussion when interpreting diffuse reflectance spectra. We would like to clarify that the Y-axis values in Fig. 2f (the original Fig. 1f) in fact represent the Kubelka-Munk function, F(R) (where F(R) = (1-R)2/2R), which is derived from the measured reflectance data and is directly proportional to the absorption coefficient of the material. It is important to note that the Kubelka-Munk function has no theoretical upper limit. Therefore, a value of ∼1.35 in the UV region is entirely expected and confirms the strong intrinsic absorption of our material in this range. As shown in the original manuscript, the Y-axis was labeled as "Absorbance (a.u.)", not reflectance.
Regarding the measurement parameters and sample preparation, the instrument used was a UV-Vis-NIR spectrophotometer (Varian Cary 500) equipped with an integrating sphere. Before measurement, baseline correction was performed using a standard barium sulfate (BaSO ) white reference. For sample preparation, the powder sample was pressed into a flat, uniform pellet in a culture dish to ensure data reliability and reproducibility. This strong absorption signal remained significant after baseline correction, further confirming its origin from the sample itself. We have added a description of these experimental details in the Supplementary Methods section.
In addition, following the reviewer's suggestion, we have provided detailed experimental methods for the monochromatic light activity tests in the revised manuscript. The monochromatic light activity tests were carried out in a dedicated reactor (PLR-PTSR II, Beijing PERFECTLIGHT) with external heating at 500 ℃. A 300 W Xenon lamp was used as the light source, coupled with optical filters to obtain monochromatic light of specific wavelengths. In each test, an optical power meter was used to accurately measure and calibrate the incident light intensity in front of the reactor window. Dividing the measured syngas generation rates by the light intensity under the corresponding monochromatic light yields the contributions of monochromatic light at different wavelength bands to the activity per unit light intensity. All other test conditions were consistent with those of the light-driven conditions.

Comment 5: The oxidation state of the catalyst under light-off conditions is a concern. The authors mention that the catalyst contacts air when the light is turned off, and Ni and Ir are prone to oxidation. However, the in situ XAS results (Fig. 2a and b) indicate non-negligible Ni-O and Ir-O signals even under illumination, suggesting that oxidized states coexist with metallic states. Reply: We thank the reviewer for their insightful comment. In our system, the NiIr nanoclusters have an average particle size of less than 1.2 nm, which leads to strong interactions with the TiO support. The in situ XAS results reflect average structural information, and at this sub-nanometer scale, it is expected that some metal atoms coordinate with oxygen from the support. Even under illumination, where Ni-Ir alloy formation occurs, a fraction of atoms particularly at the interface may still bond with surface oxygen atoms of TiO . Specifically, under light irradiation, the in situ XANES and EXAFS analyses (Fig. 3a and b, originally Fig. 2a and b) show that NiIr /TiO exhibits negligible Ir-O coordination compared to the adjacent baseline signal, with a coordination number of zero as shown in Supplementary Fig. 19-20 and Supplementary Tables 4-5, while the dominant contribution comes from Ir-Ni bonds. On the other hand, the presence of Ni-O coordination is reasonable and structurally essential, as it reflects the interfacial bonding between Ni and the TiO support. This is further corroborated by the fitting results summarized in Fig. 3c (originally Fig. 2c) and the supplementary data. As stated in the manuscript, "Under light irradiation, NiIr /TiO exhibits nearly 100% Ir-Ni coordination at the Ir L -edge and 32% Ir-Ni coordination at the Ni K-edge, alongside 37% Ni-O interfacial bonds."
Moreover, comparison with monometallic references (Supplementary Fig. 18) reveals that under identical conditions, Ni/TiO transforms almost entirely into metallic Ni-Ni bonds, whereas Ir/TiO still shows residual Ir-O coordination. The absence of Ir-O coordination in NiIr /TiO under light confirms that Ir in the alloy phase does not directly interact with TiO , while Ni maintains interfacial Ni-O bonds, forming a nano-island architecture that isolates the NiIr alloy from the support.
Regarding the reaction mechanism when the catalyst is in an oxidized state, we have included relevant discussion in the mechanism section. As noted in the manuscript, "Ox-NiIr/TiO exhibited excessive CO adsorption but poor C=O scission capacity (Supplementary Fig. 48), while thermal conditions promoted direct CH cracking into carbon deposits (Supplementary Fig. 49). This starkly contrasts with photoinduced NiIr nano-island alloy, underscoring light's critical role in structural optimization." In the absence of light, the catalyst remains in an oxidized state and follows a different reaction pathway. However, the central focus of this study is the light-driven formation of the NiIr alloy and the superior performance and reaction mechanism of this alloy compared to monometallic or oxidized counterparts. Therefore, further investigation into the reaction mechanism over the oxidized catalyst is beyond the scope of the present work.

(1) Regarding your Comment 2 (a), the statement in question was included in the introduction to provide a general background on photoinduced effects in catalytic systems, and it is supported by multiple references (Refs. 17-20). For instance, Marimuthu et al. (Ref 17, Science 339, 1590-1593 (2013)) demonstrated that plasmon-induced hot carriers and local fields lead to dynamic interconversion between metallic (Cu0) and oxidized (Cu+/Cu2+) states on Cu nanoparticles, thereby modulating reaction pathways. Lee et al. (Ref 18, Nat. Mater. 18, 620-626 (2019)) showed that localization of photogenerated electrons dynamically tunes the valence state of isolated Cu atoms, activating TiO and improving photocatalytic performance. Ye et al. (Ref 19, J. Am. Chem. Soc. 145, 20530-20538 (2023)) revealed that photoexcited charge carriers induce structural restoration of Cu/TiO from inactive Cu O to metallic Cu during methanol steam reforming. Ren et al. (Ref 20, J. Am. Chem. Soc. 145, 28276-28283 (2023)) reported that double oxygen vacancies form and recover during CO photoreduction, altering product selectivity. These studies collectively illustrate that light-driven charge redistribution can modify surface properties and induce structural dynamics.
In addition, we have now added further supporting literature to strengthen this argument:
Jiang et al. (Nat. Catal. 6, 519-530 (2023)) confirms that photoexcited electrons can weaken original metal-oxygen (M-O) bonds, leading to changes in surface structure. Wang et al. (J. Am. Chem. Soc. 147, 17, 14705-14714 (2025)) reported that Mn-induced charge transfer and photoexcited electron capture reduce the Mn valence state and weaken the La-O-Mn bond in perovskites, further illustrating how light-induced electron transfer between bimetallic sites can weaken metal-support bonds and induce structural reorganization. Prof. Xiong described a light-induced dissolution–reprecipitation process using high-entropy oxides (HEOs) as supports (Adv. Mater. 37(21), 2500928 (2025)), wherein illumination weakens metal–O bonds in the HEO, leading to Co and Ni leaching and subsequent alloy formation. Thus, the statement is well-grounded in previous and recent experimental studies.
(2) Regarding Comment 2 (b), we agree that a clear mechanistic rationale is essential and have also addressed this point in our response to Reviewer 1's Comment 2. Our experimental and computational results provide strong support for the proposed reversible bond breaking and reformation.
Firstly, we have conducted direct experimental evidence from in situ XAS. Under light, Ir L -edge EXAFS of NiIr /TiO shows a dominant Ir-Ni peak at 2.18 Å replacing the initial Ir-O coordination, while Ni K-edge EXAFS retains Ni-O and Ni-Ni paths alongside a new Ni-Ir coordination, indicating alloy formation without full Ni reduction (Fig. 3a-b). Quantitative EXAFS fitting (Fig. 3c, Supplementary Fig. 19-20, Supplementary Tables 4-5 in the revised version) shows nearly 100% Ir-Ni coordination at the Ir L -edge and 32% Ir-Ni at the Ni K-edge under light. This confirms that Ir in the alloy phase does not directly interact with TiO , while Ni maintains interfacial Ni-O bonds, forming a nano-island architecture that isolates the NiIr alloy from the support. In dark thermal conditions, limited reduction occurs and no significant Ni-Ir bonds form, proving light is essential. Furthermore, re-oxidation in post-EXAFS (Supplementary Fig. 27 and Note 4) and reversible NAP-XPS trends confirm that NiIr/TiO -L exists transiently only under light irradiation.
Secondly, we have performed DFT calculations to provide evidences. The formation energy of NiIr/TiO -L is lower than that of a hypothetical Ir-linked model (NiIr/TiO -L ), in which Ir-O bonds elongate (>3.0 Å), destabilizing the interface (Fig. 3g, Supplementary Fig. 33). Electron density distributions (Supplementary Fig. 40a-d and Note 8) show that Ni-mediated charge polarization enriches electrons at Ir sites. Density of states profiles (Supplementary Fig. 40e-h) reveal that NiIr alloy formation modulates the d-band center, optimizing the trade-off between adsorption strength and desorption kinetics. Time-dependent DFT simulations (Fig. 4i) further illustrate excitation-dependent charge redistribution in NiIr/TiO -L .
In addition, we supplemented our DFT analysis with comparative calculations of bond strengths in the excited state versus the ground state (Supplementary Table 6). The bond energy in the excited state is lower compared to the ground state. This is because photoinduced charge transfer leads to the weakening of chemical bonds, which combined with thermal effects, facilitates atomic movement towards a more stable structure. A detailed comparison reveals that in the O -NiIr/TiO structure, the difference in Ir-O bond energy between the excited state and the ground state is larger, while the difference for the Ni-O bond is smaller. This indicates that under photoexcitation, the Ir-O bond becomes more unstable and is weakened more significantly, thus it preferentially breaks, facilitating Ir migration. In addition, simulations under photoexcitation show that the Ni-Ir bond strength (92.35 kJ mol-1) in the NiIr/TiO -L alloy structure in the excited state is more stable than the Ir-O bond strength (69.64 kJ mol-1) in the excited state of the O -NiIr/TiO structure. This provides supporting evidence for the formation of the Ni-Ir alloy under light irradiation.

Comment 3: The manuscript insufficiently clarifies the origin of photogenerated electrons in NiIr/TiO -LNi under illumination. Crucially, the text fails to explicitly state:
a.What physical mechanism drives their generation?
b.What mechanism drives their generation?
Reply: We sincerely thank the reviewer for this valuable comment, which has helped us further clarify and improve the manuscript. Regarding the physical mechanism of photogenerated electron generation, it originates from the fundamental principles of photocatalysis. TiO , as a semiconductor with UV-visible light response, possesses a band structure consisting of a valence band (VB) and a conduction band (CB), separated by a bandgap. Upon irradiation with photons of energy matching or exceeding the bandgap, electrons in the VB are excited and jump to the CB, generating electron-hole pairs. These photogenerated charge carriers then migrate to the catalyst surface, where they drive the catalytic reactions. Under concentrated light intensity, the NiIr alloy can be further excited, generate hot electrons, and contribute to a local temperature rise. While both photoelectric and photothermal effects are present and synergistic, the controlled condensation experiments (Fig. 2e) confirm that the photoelectric effect plays a more dominant role.
Concerning the electron transfer pathway, our comprehensive mechanistic investigations have clearly demonstrated a support-Ni-Ir electron transfer pathway under illumination. In situ NAP-XPS analyses provide direct evidence of this light-induced electron transfer. The Ir 4f spectra (Fig. 3d-e) reveal a pronounced shift toward lower binding energy, with the Ir0 fraction increasing from 36.96% (dark) to 60.65%. Upon switching to focused light, the Ir0 fraction further rises to 62.31%. This indicates that Ir gains electrons under irradiation. Parallel in situ Ni 2p NAP-XPS (Supplementary Fig. 24a-c) shows analogous trends, with Ni0/Ni2+ ratios tracking Ir's redox dynamics. While Ti 2p and O 1s exhibit the positive shift in the binding energy of Ti and O under light irradiation (Supplementary Fig. 24d-e), this demonstrates that electrons migrate from the TiO support to Ni-Ir under illumination. Subsequently, electrons are further transferred from Ni to Ir. In situ XAS analysis (Fig. 3a-c, Supplementary Fig. 19-20, and Supplementary Tables 4-5) also supports this mechanism. It reveals that Ir in the alloy phase does not directly interact with TiO , while Ni maintains interfacial Ni-O bonds, forming a nano-island structure that isolates the NiIr alloy from the support. This configuration formation indicates the electron transfer from Ni to Ir under light irradiation. Additionally, time-dependent DFT (TD-DFT) simulations (Fig. 4i) show that electrons in photoexcited states preferentially accumulate at Ir sites distal to the TiO interface. S →S promotes hole accumulation at Ni sites alongside electron enrichment at Ir sites, a spatial charge segregation that drives photoexcited electrons toward Ir centers in higher-energy states.
Comment 4: The positive and negative values of the Mulliken charges analysis should be explained.
Reply: We sincerely thank the reviewer for this valuable comment, which has helped us further clarify and improve the manuscript. In Mulliken population analysis, the calculated atomic charge reflects the balance between the number of valence electrons associated with an atom in the isolated state and the electron density assigned to it within the molecule or solid. Positive Mulliken charge indicates that the atom has lost electron density relative to its neutral atomic state. This is commonly interpreted as electron donation toward neighboring atoms or into the bonding network, consistent with an electron-deficient or partially oxidized character. Negative Mulliken charge signifies that the atom has gained electron density, i.e., it has accepted charge from its surroundings. Such atoms are considered electron-rich or partially reduced relative to their neutral state. It should be noted that Mulliken charges are semi-quantitative and mainly used to capture relative charge-transfer trends rather than absolute electron counts. We have added the corresponding explanation in the supplementary information to further enhance the clarity of this analysis.
Revision made: The following contents have been revised in Supplementary Information:
Mulliken charge analysis quantifies distinct patterns of interfacial charge redistribution: Positive charges indicate electron density loss relative to the neutral atom, reflecting electron donation to the neighbors or bonding network. Negative charges signify electron density gain from the surroundings, indicating an electron-rich/partially reduced character.
(Please refer to the marked content on page 42 in the supplementary information.)
Comment 5: For the proposed reaction pathways, critical bond-breaking steps (e.g., *CO → *CO*O, *CH → *H*CH ) require transition state analysis with corresponding energy barriers. Without these kinetic validations, the mechanistic pathway lacks practical significance and fails to establish a credible catalytic cycle.
Reply: We sincerely thank the reviewer for this valuable comment, which has helped us further clarify and improve the manuscript. As rightly noted, the initial bond cleavage of CO and CH is indeed a critical step in DRM. In response, we have supplemented the transition state analysis in our revised manuscript as suggested. For the initial bond cleavage of CO and CH molecules, as shown in the updated Fig. 5a-b and Supplementary Figs. 43-44, NiIr/TiO -L demonstrates both thermodynamic and kinetic advantages. Compared to monometallic Ni/TiO and Ir/TiO , NiIr/TiO -L exhibits a significantly greater energy reduction after direct C=O scission of CO and the first C-H scission of CH , indicating superior thermodynamic favorability. Furthermore, NiIr/TiO -L exhibits transition state activation energies (Ea) of +0.26 eV for C=O scission and +0.30 eV for C-H scission. These values are lower than the corresponding transition state barriers on both Ni/TiO and Ir/TiO , clearly indicating the kinetic advantage of the nanoisland NiIr alloy. To clearly present these new kinetic validations, we have also accordingly reorganized the panel structure of Fig. 5 (the original Fig. 4).
Revision made: The following contents have been revised in Manuscript and Supplementary Information:
For the initial bond cleavage of CO and CH molecules as shown in Fig. 5a-b and Supplementary Figs. 43-44, NiIr/TiO -L demonstrates both thermodynamic and kinetic advantages. Compared to monometallic Ni/TiO and Ir/TiO , NiIr/TiO -L exhibits a significantly greater energy reduction after direct C=O scission of CO and the first C-H scission of CH , indicating its superior thermodynamic favorability. Meanwhile, NiIr/TiO -L exhibits activation energies (Ea) of the transition states at +0.26 eV for C=O scission and +0.30 eV for C-H scission. These values are lower than the transition state barriers for the first C-H scission of CH and direct CO scission on Ni/TiO and Ir/TiO , indicating the kinetic advantage of the nanoisland NiIr alloy. Supplementary Fig. 45 further compares the pathway of direct C=O scission of CO with the indirect activation route via COOH pathways. The results reveal Ir/TiO 's propensity for *COOH formation, aligning with in situ SR-DRIFTS detected RWGS activity and a suboptimal H /CO ratio. In contrast, NiIr/TiO -L enables concerted C=O scission, where Ni site stabilizes dissociative oxygen and Ir site coordinates carbon, directly yielding CO and *O species.
Regarding the subsequent activation process after the initial bond cleavage of CH , *CH may undergo further direct C-H scission until a C atom remains. Alternatively, *CH can be assisted by activation through combination with O species from CO activation (O ) or lattice oxygen (O ). Fig. 5c compares the thermodynamic energy changes before and after the reaction for these three possible activation pathways. The results show that the sequential direct C-H scission pathway (*CH3→*CH2→*CH→*C) on NiIr/TiO -L requires prohibitively high energy, particularly 1.18 eV for cleaving the second C-H bond. For the *O-assisted C-H scission routes, O -assisted pathways proved unfavorable due to the high *CH migration energy of 1.30 eV. Conversely, *O species from CO dissociation adsorbed on Ni sites in NiIr/TiO -L enabled thermodynamically favorable *CH O formation with ΔE = -0.61 eV, and subsequent dehydrogenation required only 0.29 eV, consistent with isotopic labeling results. Comparative studies between NiIr/TiO -L and monometallic Ni/TiO and Ir/TiO in Supplementary Fig. 46 further highlight the optimal performance of NiIr/TiO -L . Specifically, in *O -assisted pathways, while Ni/TiO struggled with CH activation exhibiting a second C-H barrier of 0.75 eV and Ir/TiO suffered from poor *O stabilization, the NiIr alloy achieved balanced kinetics through asymmetric Ni-Ir sites.

Comment 6: For Fig.4c, regardless of the catalyst structure employed, since reactants and products remain identical, the energy of initial and final states should be identical relative to those reactants and products.
Reply: We appreciate the reviewer's thoughtful comment regarding the energy reference used in Fig. 5 (the original Fig.4). We fully agree with the thermodynamic statement that, for the reaction CH + CO → 2CO + 2H , the overall reaction energy must be identical across catalysts when the initial and final states are defined as gas-phase reactants and gas-phase products with a fully restored (clean) surface. Under this unified reference, the catalyst energy cancels out and the net reaction energy depends only on the molecular species.
The goal of Fig. 5c (the original Fig.4b) is to establish that the O-assisted C-H scission pathway, in which an oxygen atom generated by prior CO dissociation participates in breaking the C-H bond, is energetically much more favorable than the direct removal of the second hydrogen from CH . Motivated by this result, Supplementary Fig. 46 (the original Fig.4c) and Fig. 5d focuses exclusively on comparing the elementary-step energetics along the O-assisted pathway on three catalysts. Accordingly, in Fig. 5c, the initial state corresponds to a clean surface; however, in the third (iii) step, an oxygen atom generated from CO dissociation (O ) is introduced to demonstrate the oxygen-assisted C–H bond activation mechanism. Therefore, the adsorption energy difference of the oxygen species derived from CO dissociation is also incorporated into the overall energy variation of this system.
The reaction sequence reads: (i) CH adsorption → (ii) the first C-H scission to *CH + *H → (iii) coupling of *CH with *O to *CH O → (iv–vi) stepwise dehydrogenation to *adsorbed CO. The *desorption of CO and surface restoration are not included in Supplementary Fig. 46 (the original Fig.4c), because the panel is designed to highlight stepwise energetics rather than the full thermodynamic cycle. The energy change of an elementary step is thus the difference between two successive states (ΔE = E - E ). For example, on Ni/TiO the CH adsorption is endothermic by +0.12 eV, and the subsequent C-H scission reduces the energy from +0.12 to -0.26 eV, i.e., -0.38 eV for that step. These vertical drops between adjacent plateaus are precisely what we compare across catalysts to quantify the driving force differences for the O-assisted C-H activation.
Because the third step in Supplementary Fig. 46 (the original Fig.4c) explicitly introduces the adsorption energy of oxygen (O) and the terminal state (adsorbed CO) is also an adsorbed state, variations in the adsorption strength and interfacial bonding of O and CO among different catalysts naturally lead to differences in their absolute energies. Therefore, the start-to-end offsets in Supplementary Fig. 46 (the original Fig.4c) are not expected to be identical. This is fully consistent with the purpose of the figure, which is to compare the energetics of elementary steps under an O-covered surface condition rather than to depict a complete thermodynamic reaction profile.
Comment 7: CO has a linear configuration in its free state, While all adsorbed CO species in this study exhibit a bent (V-shaped) geometry.
Reply: We thank the reviewer for this insightful comment. The reviewer is correct that the free CO molecule in the gas phase exhibits a linear geometry. However, all configurations shown in our study represent CO molecules in the adsorbed state. Upon adsorption onto the catalyst surface, CO undergoes significant electronic and structural changes due to interaction with the active sites. Specifically, charge transfer and orbital rehybridization between CO and the catalyst lead to a bending of the O-C-O angle, which is a well-established indicator of CO activation in heterogeneous catalysis. This bent configuration corresponds to a chemisorbed and activated state of CO , which is a crucial precursor step facilitating its subsequent conversion. Therefore, the observed V-shaped geometry in our models is consistent with the expected behavior of activated CO in catalytic systems and validates the effectiveness of the considered catalysts in promoting CO activation. This behavior is consistent with many previous theoretical findings in CO activation studies (Angew. Chem. Int. Ed. 58, 6916 (2019), doi.org/10.1002/anie.201900565; J. Am. Chem. Soc. 142, 3214-3221 (2020), doi.org/10.1021/jacs.9b13280; J. Phys. Chem. C 123, 6516-6525(2019), doi.org/10.1021/acs.jpcc.8b11816; ACS Catal. 15, 2916-2926 (2025), doi.org/10.1021/acscatal.4c07178).
